webchanges vs urlwatch: a comparison

Both tools watch web pages, browser-rendered pages and the output of shell commands for changes, and notify you. webchanges began as a fork of urlwatch and runs urlwatch's jobs and configuration files as they are — then adds four high-value things urlwatch can't do, and many smaller ones.

Bottom line: Pick webchanges if you need any of TLS/JA3 fingerprint evasion for sites with bot walls, AI-summarized diffs of long documents, image change detection, or structural JSON/XML diffs without false alarms — or simply a tool that is actively developed. Switching takes one command and leaves your urlwatch setup untouched.

The 4 high-value wins

If any of these match what you monitor, urlwatch can't keep up. Each is a webchanges feature with no urlwatch equivalent.

1Get past TLS/JA3 fingerprinting curl_cffi

Why it matters: Cloudflare, Akamai, DataDome and friends fingerprint the TLS handshake and the HTTP/2 settings, not just the User-Agent. urlwatch's requests client gets a 403 with no recourse; webchanges can go through curl_cffi with a real browser's TLS profile.

How: set http_client: curl_cffi and impersonate: chrome (or safari / firefox / edge). Override fingerprints.ja3, fingerprints.akamai and fingerprints.extra_fp, or pin http_version (up to v3only). 

url: https://hard-to-scrape.example/
http_client: curl_cffi
impersonate: chrome
http_version: v2tls

2Long diffs → one paragraph ai_google

Why it matters: watching 50 pages of terms of service, an RFC draft, a regulatory filing or a long policy? webchanges sends you a plain-language summary of what changed, ahead of the diff, instead of only a 2,000-line patch. urlwatch sends the raw patch and leaves the reading to you.

How: differ: ai_google calls Google's Gemini with a prompt template that can use {old_text}, {new_text} and {unified_diff}. Set the model, system_instructions, temperature, top_p, thinking_budget or thinking_level. Bring your own (free) Gemini API key. 

differ:
  name: ai_google
  prompt: 'Summarize material changes by section.\n\n{unified_diff}'

3Watch images, not just text image

Why it matters: logo swaps, product-photo updates, chart images, status-page banners. urlwatch only compares text, so if the content is an image you're out of luck. webchanges highlights what changed in yellow on a greyscale copy of the image, right in the HTML report.

How: differ: image with data_type: url (or filename / ascii85 / base64), and mse_threshold (default 2.5) to ignore compression noise. Add ai_google to also get a description of the change. In BETA. 

url: https://example.com/logo.png
filters:
  - ascii85
differ:
  name: image
  data_type: ascii85
  mse_threshold: 5.0

4JSON/XML diffs that don't cry wolf deepdiff

Why it matters: APIs reorder arrays, numbers drift in the last decimal, and a one-field change turns into a wall of reformatted lines. urlwatch compares the serialized text and pings you for noise; you end up chaining format-json, jq and a custom diff_tool and still miss nested changes. webchanges compares the parsed structure, element by element.

How: differ: deepdiff with data_type: json (or yaml / xml), ignore_order, ignore_string_case, significant_digits and compact. 

differ:
  name: deepdiff
  data_type: json
  ignore_order: true
  significant_digits: 2

Use webchanges if…

  • Any of the four wins above apply.
  • You want reports you can read at a glance: HTML reports keep the page's formatting and clickable links, mark additions and deletions in color (also in Gmail and in dark mode), and can show changes side by side (table) or word by word (wdiff).
  • You need fine control of the browser: block_elements, evaluate, chained wait_for_*, a persistent user_data_dir, switches, http_credentials, or attaching to a browser that is already running (connect_over_cdp).
  • You want fewer false alarms: empty_as_error treats an empty response as a transient error, suppress_repeated_errors reports an error once instead of at every run, and same_site_delay spaces out the jobs hitting the same site.
  • You want reporters that earn their keep: github_issue turns each change into a tracked issue with labels, assignees and milestone; browser opens the HTML report locally; run_command passes {count}, {jobs} and {text} plus the WEBCHANGES_*_JSON environment variables; telegram keeps bold, italics, strikethrough and links.
  • You want snapshots you can trust: they are saved only after the reports have been sent; max_snapshots caps the database's growth; and --rollback-database undoes a bad filter change.
  • You want tools for maintaining your jobs: --errors lists the jobs that fail or capture nothing, --test without a job checks every file, and editors autocomplete and validate jobs.yaml and config.yaml from the JSON Schemas webchanges installs.
  • You keep jobs in several files (globs and directories, with --jobs or the jobs configuration directive), or want secrets kept out of them (!env).
  • You want extra filters: execute (runs a program without a shell), between, absolute_links, format-xml, jsontoyaml, xmltojson, xmltoyaml, ascii85, base64, pypdf, remove_repeated, and keep_lines_containing / delete_lines_containing with text or re.
  • You need HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) to reach a site.

Switching from urlwatch

Install webchanges and run webchanges --test. On its first run it copies urlwatch's files from ~/.urlwatch (or urlwatch's default directory, e.g. ~/.config/urlwatch): urls.yaml becomes jobs.yaml, urlwatch.yaml becomes config.yaml, and the snapshot database is converted once (with the minidb package). urlwatch's own files are left untouched, so you can switch back at any time.

Keeps working as is

  • Browser jobs: navigate, useragent, browser, wait_until, wait_for
  • filter, diff_filter, diff_tool, http_proxy, https_proxy, json, kind: shell, treat_new_as_changed, and stderr with all four values
  • Filters grep, grepi, and html2text methods pyhtml2text, re and lynx (which uses the default method)
  • Reporters slack, mattermost and shell
  • --urls, --cache, --gc-cache, --test-filter, --test-diff-filter, --enable, --disable, and selecting a job by index, name or URL/command

The renamed ones print a deprecation warning, to update when convenient.

Needs a change

  • hooks.py: import from webchanges instead of urlwatch, and adapt custom classes to the hooks API.
  • --tags work home becomes --tags work,home.

Looks different

  • html2text without a method converts to Markdown (urlwatch only removed the tags); add method: strip_tags to keep urlwatch's output.
  • Only the latest 4 snapshots of each job are kept; set max_snapshots: 0 to keep all.
  • Telegram reports are sent in Markdown, so monospace has no effect.

Full reference comparison

Source: each project's code and reference docs (webchanges 3.39, urlwatch 2.29).

Jobs & universal directives

Directive webchanges urlwatch Notes
name, enabled, kind, user_visible_url, compared_versions, max_tries, tags, treat_new_as_changed, stderr (command jobs) ✓ ✓ Common ground. stderr: forward is urlwatch's stderr: urlwatch, which also works.
filter / filters, diff_filter / diff_filters ✓ ✓ Plural in webchanges; the singular still works.
differ — typed differ selector with sub-directives ✓ × urlwatch only has diff_tool (an external command).
additions_only, deletions_only ✓ × Report only what was added (e.g. new items in a list), or only what was removed.
suppress_errors / suppress_repeated_errors / suppress_error_ended ✓ × Mute errors, repeated errors, or the notice that an error has ended.
empty_as_error ✓ × Treat an empty response as a transient error instead of a change.
same_site_delay ✓ × Spaces out the jobs hitting the same site, to stay clear of rate limits.
note, monospace, is_markdown, markdown_extras, contextlines ✓ × Per-job report rendering.
hook_data ✓ × Any data for your hooks.py code.
!env YAML tag ✓ × Inserts environment variables (e.g. secrets) into any value of the jobs and configuration files.

Capability webchanges urlwatch

http_version: v1, v2, v2tls, v2_prior_knowledge, v3, v3only ✓ ×
impersonate (chrome / safari / firefox / edge) ✓ ×
fingerprints: ja3, akamai, extra_fp ✓ ×
params, retries, no_redirects, no_conditional_request, ignore_dh_key_too_small ✓ ×
data_as_json ✓ json
Common: headers, cookies, data, method, encoding, timeout, ssl_no_verify, ignore_cached, proxy (urlwatch: http_proxy / https_proxy), ignore_connection_errors, ignore_http_error_codes, ignore_timeout_errors, ignore_too_many_redirects, ignore_incomplete_reads ✓ ✓

Browser jobs (Playwright)

Both projects drive the browser with Playwright. urlwatch launches Playwright's bundled Chromium, Firefox or WebKit with a handful of directives; webchanges uses an installed Chrome or Edge (any release channel), Firefox or WebKit, and exposes far more of Playwright.

webchanges — use_browser: true

  • block_elements (skip stylesheets, images, fonts, media, scripts…)
  • connect_over_cdp (attach to an already-running browser over the DevTools Protocol)
  • evaluate (run JavaScript and use its result)
  • init_script, initialization_url, initialization_js (prepare the page before going to the URL)
  • switches, ignore_default_args, user_data_dir (control how the browser is launched)
  • http_credentials, proxy (log in, also to a proxy)
  • ignore_https_errors, referer, headers, cookies
  • wait_for_function, wait_for_selector (state, strict, timeout; one or a list), wait_for_url, wait_for_timeout, wait_until

urlwatch — navigate:

  • navigate, wait_until, wait_for, useragent, browser, ignore_http_error_codes

Same engine, much smaller set of controls. webchanges runs these jobs as they are, translating useragent into a User-Agent header, browser into use_browser and wait_for into wait_for_selector.

Filters

Both share the core: CSS and XPath selectors, element-by-*, html2text, beautify, csv2text, ical2text, pdf2text, ocr, jq, format-json, pretty-xml, re.sub, re.findall, sort, reverse, sha1sum, hexdump and shellpipe. The differences are webchanges' additions:

  • webchanges-only: execute (runs a program without a shell, safer than shellpipe), between, absolute_links, format-xml, jsontoyaml, xmltojson, xmltoyaml, ascii85, base64, pypdf, sha256sum, remove_repeated; a strip with chars, side and splitlines; and pdf2text with raw and physical.
  • Renamed in webchanges (the old names still work): grep → keep_lines_containing, grepi → delete_lines_containing (both take text or re), striplines → strip with splitlines: true, remove-duplicate-lines → remove_repeated.
  • html2text converts to Markdown by default in webchanges (with the Python html2text package); urlwatch's default only strips the tags, which webchanges does with method: strip_tags.

Command-line interface

webchanges accepts urlwatch's arguments (the renamed ones under their old names too) and adds tools for testing, maintaining jobs, managing the database and troubleshooting.

Flag What it does webchanges urlwatch
--tags, --enable, --disable, --prepare-jobs, --change-location, --dump-history, --test-reporter, --smtp-login, --xmpp-login, --telegram-chats, --edit-config, --edit-hooks, --features Common ground; each argument that takes a job selects it by index, name or URL/command. ✓ ✓
--jobs, --hooks Load several files: repeat the argument, or give a glob or a directory. ✓ one file
--errors [REPORTER] Run every enabled job and list those that fail or capture no data; optionally send the list to a reporter. ✓ ×
--list-jobs [REGEX] List jobs and their index numbers, optionally only those matching a regular expression. ✓ --list, no filter
--test [JOB] Run one job and show its filtered output. Without a JOB, check the configuration, jobs and hooks files for errors. ✓ --test-filter, JOB required
--test-differ JOB Replay the differ over the saved snapshots; with --test-reporter, preview the result in any reporter. ✓ --test-diff-filter
--no-headless Show the browser window of browser jobs (to debug captchas, redirects, login walls). ✓ ×
--max-workers N Cap the number of jobs run in parallel. ✓ ×
--gc-database [N] Delete the snapshots of jobs no longer in the jobs file and keep the latest N of the others (default 1). ✓ --gc-cache
--clean-database [N] Keep only the latest N snapshots of every job (default 1), and compact the database. ✓ ×
--rollback-database TIMESTAMP Delete every snapshot saved after TIMESTAMP — the undo for a bad filter that set off a wave of false changes. ✓ ×
--delete-snapshot JOB Delete a job's latest snapshot, e.g. to have a change reported again. ✓ ×
--database-engine, --max-snapshots N Override the database engine and retention without editing config.yaml. ✓ ×
--footnote "TEXT" Add a footnote to the reports. ✓ ×
--log-file FILE Write the log to a file (implies -v). ✓ ×
--check-new Check PyPI for a newer release of webchanges. ✓ ×
--detailed-versions Show the versions of webchanges, Python, SQLite, every dependency and the browser — useful for bug reports. ✓ ×
--install-chrome Install or update the Chrome browser used by browser jobs. ✓ ×

Configuration & database

  • Configuration items only in webchanges: differ_defaults (defaults for each differ), database (engine and max_snapshots), footnote, and jobs / hooks (which files to load: files, globs or directories). Keys starting with _ (e.g. _note:) are remarks.
  • Database: both offer SQLite-based, Redis and text-file storage. webchanges' default SQLite database is indexed and compressed, keeps the latest 4 snapshots of each job (urlwatch keeps them all), and is written only after the reports have been sent.
  • Default locations of the files — webchanges: Linux ~/.config/webchanges, macOS ~/Library/Application Support/webchanges, Windows %USERPROFILE%\Documents\webchanges. urlwatch's are found automatically on the first run.

FAQ

What's the single biggest reason to choose webchanges?

Its differs: ai_google turns a 2,000-line legal diff into a paragraph, deepdiff ends false alarms on JSON and XML, and image watches pictures. urlwatch has none of these.

Can webchanges scrape sites that block urlwatch?

Often, yes. Use http_client: curl_cffi with impersonate: chrome (or safari / firefox / edge), and override fingerprints.ja3 / fingerprints.akamai if needed. urlwatch has no fingerprinting controls.

Is migrating from urlwatch hard?

No. webchanges reads urlwatch's jobs and configuration files as they are, copies them on its first run, and converts the snapshot database once. urlwatch's own files are left untouched, so you can switch back at any time. Only custom hooks.py code needs adapting; see Switching from urlwatch.

Does webchanges send my pages to Google?

Only if you opt in to the ai_google differ, which needs your own Gemini API key. Otherwise everything runs on your machine.
